evidence.claim: East of Tolland center, modern Route 74 follows part of the Tolland County Turnpike, laid out in 1809.
evidence.quote: The eastern half of modern Route 74 (east of Tolland center) was originally laid out as a turnpike in 1809 known as the Tolland County Turnpike.

evidence.claim: The company collected tolls until it dissolved in 1834.
evidence.quote: The turnpike corporation collected tolls until 1834 when the corporation was dissolved.

evidence.claim: In 1922, the road from Rockville to Tolland and the turnpike route onward to West Ashford became State Highway 107.
evidence.quote: In 1922, the turnpike route between Tolland and West Ashford and the road between Rockville and Tolland was designated as State Highway 107.

evidence.claim: The 1932 state highway renumbering made old Highway 107 Route 74.
evidence.quote: Route 74 was commissioned in the 1932 state highway renumbering from old Highway 107

evidence.claim: Approaching from Rockville, Route 74 heads east toward Tolland, where it briefly shares Route 30.
evidence.quote: When Route 83 turns to the north at West Street, Route 74 continues eastward towards Tolland. In Tolland, Route 74 continues east through town, with a brief concurrency with Route 30.

evidence.quote: On either side of the Green at the south end are two town halls

evidence.claim: On the west side, the former courthouse became the town library in 1899, after most county courts moved to Rockville in 1890.
evidence.quote: The courthouse remained in service as such until 1890, when county courts mostly moved to Rockville. Starting in 1899, the courthouse housed the town's public library.

evidence.claim: On the west side, the former courthouse
evidence.quote: The Old Tolland County Courthouse is located on the west side of the Tolland Green

evidence.claim: A square tower base, octagonal belfry and round cupola rise above the old courthouse.
evidence.quote: The roof is topped by a two-story tower, with a square base and an octagonal louvered belfry capped by a round cupola.

evidence.claim: Built in 1822, it remained in service until most county courts moved to Rockville in 1890.
evidence.quote: The courthouse was built in 1822, when Tolland was the county seat of Tolland County. The courthouse remained in service as such until 1890, when county courts mostly moved to Rockville.

evidence.claim: The town library occupied it from 1899 to 1985.
evidence.quote: It housed the Tolland Public Library from 1899 to 1985.

evidence.claim: In 1930, Samuel Simpson bought the building for one dollar and donated it to the library association.
evidence.quote: In 1930, the courthouse was sold for $1 to Samuel Simpson, who promptly donated the building to the Tolland Public Library Association.

evidence.claim: The association gave it to the Tolland Historical Society in 2001 for restoration and conversion into a museum.
evidence.quote: In 2001, the Tolland Public Library Association donated the courthouse to the Tolland Historical Society, which oversaw its restoration and conversion to a museum.

evidence.claim: The restored second floor resembles its original courtroom.
evidence.quote: The interior has been restored, with the second floor resembling its original appearance as a courtroom.

evidence.claim: The stone section built in 1856 was already the fourth jail on this site.
evidence.quote: Its earliest section, made of stone and built in 1856, was in fact the fourth jail built on that site.

evidence.claim: It held people convicted of crimes and people awaiting trial at the courthouse across the street.
evidence.quote: The Jail served as the county jail in the 19th and 20th century for criminals who were convicted of a crime or were awaiting a trial at the courthouse across the street.

evidence.claim: A hotel in front, the County House, accommodated visitors with jail or court business until fire destroyed it in 1893.
evidence.quote: The jail also had a hotel in front until a fire burned it down in 1893.  The hotel, known as the County House, was used to provide hospitality to visitors who had jail or court related business.

evidence.claim: That year, a brick addition doubled the cells from 16 to 32.
evidence.quote: In 1893, a brick section was added, doubling the number of cells from 16 to 32.

evidence.claim: The jail remained in use until 1968.
evidence.quote: The present jail was in use from 1856 to 1968.

evidence.claim: The Tolland Historical Society now operates the building as a museum.
evidence.quote: The building is now operated as a museum by the Tolland Historical Society.

evidence.claim: The Hicks-Stearns house began as a tavern in 1788.
evidence.quote: The house was built in 1788, when it served as a tavern.

evidence.claim: The Hicks family occupied it from 1845 to 1970.
evidence.quote: It was occupied by the Hicks family from 1845 until 1970.

evidence.claim: Ratcliffe Hicks expanded the house with a front porch and three-story tower, adding Victorian elements to the earlier building.
evidence.quote: Ratcliffe renovated and expanded the family house with many Victorian elements, adding a front porch and a distinctive three-story tower.

evidence.claim: His daughter Elizabeth left the family home to a nonprofit trust for conversion into a museum.
evidence.quote: Elizabeth willed the Tolland family home to a nonprofit trust to convert into a museum.

evidence.claim: A colonial kitchen and Victorian parlor now share the house.
evidence.quote: The Hicks-Stearns family house is a transition home, featuring a colonial-era kitchen and a Victorian-era parlor and furnishings.

evidence.claim: The collections include family heirlooms, a Victrola and faux bamboo furniture, alongside the furnished parlor.
evidence.quote: Collections include family heirlooms, cloth tea balls, Victrola, and faux bamboo furniture.

evidence.claim: His daughter Elizabeth
evidence.quote: Ratcliffe's daughter, painter and philanthropist Elizabeth Hicks

evidence.claim: The exterior has clapboards and a Palladian window beneath the gabled roof.
evidence.quote: with a gabled roof and clapboarded exterior with a Palladian window.

evidence.claim: County administration ran the jail until 1960, when the state government took over.
evidence.quote: Management of the jail remained in the hands of the county administration until 1960, when it was transferred to the state government.

evidence.claim: Ratcliffe’s work extended beyond the house: he was a lawyer, industrialist and Connecticut state legislator.
evidence.quote: successful lawyer and industrialist (president of the Canfield Rubber Works in Bridgeport), and Connecticut state legislator.
